title: VIII. Over The Brandy
paragraphs: The argument was over. But, strangely enough, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who'd been in such high spirits, suddenly began to frown. He frowned and gulped down brandy -- and it was already one glass too many.

"Get out of here, you Jesuits!" he shouted at the servants. "Go away, Smerdyakov. I'll send you the gold piece I promised you today, but be off! Don't cry, Grigory. Go to Marfa, she'll comfort you and put you to bed. The rascals won't even let us sit in peace after dinner," he snapped irritably, as the servants promptly withdrew at his word.
"Smerdyakov always pokes his way in now, after dinner. You're the one he's so interested in. What have you done to fascinate him?" he added, turning to Ivan.
"Nothing whatever," Ivan answered. "He's pleased to think highly of me; he's a lackey, and a shabby soul. Raw material for revolution, though, when the time comes."
"For revolution?"
"There'll be others, better ones. But there'll be some like him too. His kind will come first, and better ones after."
"And when will that time come?"
"The rocket will go up and fizzle out, most likely. The peasants aren't too fond of listening to these soup-makers yet, at least not so far."
"Ah, brother, but a Balaam's ass like that thinks and thinks, and God only knows where he'll end up."
"He's storing up ideas," said Ivan, smiling.

"You see, I know he can't stand me, or anyone else, even you, though you imagine he thinks highly of you. Worse still with Alyosha -- he despises Alyosha. But he doesn't steal, that's one thing in his favor, and he's no gossip, he holds his tongue, doesn't air our dirty linen in public. He makes a capital fish pie, too. But damn him, is he really worth all this talk?"
"Of course he isn't."

"And as for whatever ideas he might be hatching -- the Russian peasant, generally speaking, needs a good thrashing. That's what I've always maintained. Our peasants are swindlers, and don't deserve any pity, and it's a good thing they're still flogged sometimes. Russia's rich in birch trees. If we ever cut down the forests, it'd be the ruin of Russia. I stand up for clever people. We've stopped thrashing the peasants -- we've grown too refined for that -- but they go right on thrashing each other. And a good thing too. 'For with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again,' or however it goes. Anyway, it'll be measured out to them. But Russia's all swinishness, through and through. My dear boy, if you only knew how much I hate Russia.... That is, not Russia itself, but all this vice! But maybe I do mean Russia. Tout cela c'est de la cochonnerie.... Do you know what I like? I like wit."
"You've had another glass. That's enough."

"Wait a bit. I'll have one more, then another, and then I'll stop. No, wait, you interrupted me. Back at Mokroe I was talking to an old man, and he told me: 'There's nothing we like so much as sentencing girls to a thrashing, and we always give the lads the job of doing it. And the girl he's thrashed today, the young man will propose to tomorrow. So it suits the girls just fine, too,' he said. There's a set of de Sades for you! But it's clever all the same. Shall we go over and have a look at that sort of thing sometime, eh? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don't be bashful, child. I'm sorry I didn't stay to dinner at the Superior's and tell the monks all about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don't be angry that I offended your Superior this morning. I lost my temper. If there is a God, if he exists, then of course I'm to blame, and I'll have to answer for it. But if there's no God at all, then what do your fathers deserve? It's not enough to cut their heads off, since they hold back progress. Would you believe it, Ivan, that all this really tears at my feelings? No, I can see you don't believe it, from your eyes. You believe what people say -- that I'm nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I'm nothing but a buffoon?"
"No, I don't believe it."

"And I believe that you don't, and that you're speaking the truth. You look sincere, and you speak sincerely. But not Ivan. Ivan's supercilious.... I'd still put an end to your monks, all the same. I'd take that whole mystical business and stamp it out, once and for all, everywhere in Russia, to bring all the fools to their senses. And think of the gold and silver that would come pouring into the mint!"
"But why suppress it?" asked Ivan.
"So that Truth may prevail. That's why."
"Well, if Truth were to prevail, you know, you'd be the very first one robbed and suppressed."

"Ah! I daresay you're right. Ah, what an ass I am!" Fyodor Pavlovitch burst out, striking himself lightly on the forehead. "Well, your monastery can stand then, Alyosha, if that's how it is. And we clever people will sit snug and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, it must have been ordained that way by the Almighty himself. Ivan, tell me -- is there a God, or isn't there? Wait, tell me the truth, tell me seriously. Why are you laughing again?"
"I'm laughing because you made such a clever remark just now, about Smerdyakov's belief in the existence of two saints who could move mountains."
"Why, am I like him now, then?"
"Very much so."

"Well, that just shows I'm a Russian too, and I've got a Russian characteristic in me. And you might get caught the same way, philosopher though you are. Want to bet I'll catch you at it tomorrow? Tell me anyway -- is there a God, or isn't there? Only be serious. I want you to be serious now."
"No, there is no God."
"Alyosha, is there a God?"
"There is."
"Ivan, and is there any kind of immortality -- just a little, just a tiny bit?"
"There's no immortality either."
"None at all?"
"None at all."
"So it's absolute nothingness, then. Or maybe there's just something? Anything's better than nothing!"
"Absolute nothingness."
"Alyosha, is there immortality?"
"There is."
"God and immortality?"
"God and immortality. Immortality is in God."

"Hm! It's more likely Ivan's right. Good Lord, to think how much faith, how much strength of every kind, mankind has poured out for nothing, on that dream, and for how many thousand years. Who's it who's laughing at man? Ivan! For the last time, once and for all -- is there a God, or isn't there? I'm asking you for the last time!"
"And for the last time -- there isn't."
"Who's laughing at mankind, Ivan?"
"It must be the devil," said Ivan, smiling.
"And the devil? Does he exist?"
"No, there's no devil either."
"That's a pity. Damn it all, what wouldn't I do to the man who first invented God! Hanging on a bitter aspen tree would be too good for him."
"There'd have been no civilization at all if they hadn't invented God."
"Wouldn't there have been? Without God?"
"No. And there'd have been no brandy either. But I really must take your brandy away from you now."
"Stop, stop, stop, dear boy, just one more little glass. I've hurt Alyosha's feelings. You're not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!"
"No, I'm not angry. I know your thoughts. Your heart is better than your head."
"My heart better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And that, from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?"
"Yes."

"You must love him" (Fyodor Pavlovitch was very drunk by this point). "Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was worked up. Still, there's something witty about that elder, don't you think, Ivan?"
"Very likely."

"There is, there is. Il y a du Piron là-dedans. He's a Jesuit, a Russian one, mind you. Being an honorable man, he's got some hidden indignation boiling inside him at having to keep up the pretense of holiness."
"But he believes in God, of course."

"Not a bit of it. Didn't you know? Why, he tells everyone so himself. That is, not everyone -- just the clever people who come to see him. He said straight out to Governor Schultz not long ago: 'Credo, but I don't know in what.'"
"Really?"

"He really did say that. But I respect him. There's something of Mephistopheles about him, or rather of 'The Hero of Our Time' -- Arbenin, or whatever his name is.... You see, he's a sensualist. Such a sensualist, in fact, that I'd be afraid for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he invited us to tea, tea with liqueur -- the ladies send him liqueur -- and started telling us about the old days until we nearly split our sides laughing.... Especially about the time he cured a paralyzed woman. 'If my legs weren't so bad, I know a dance I could show you,' he said. What do you make of that? 'I've had plenty of tricks up my sleeve in my time,' he said. He swindled Demidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand."
"What, he stole it?"

"He brought him the money like a man he trusted, saying, 'Take care of this for me, friend, there'll be a police search at my place tomorrow.' And he kept it. 'You gave it to the Church,' he told him. I said to him: 'You're a scoundrel,' I said. 'No,' he said, 'I'm not a scoundrel, I'm just broad-minded.' But that wasn't him -- that was someone else. I've mixed him up with someone else... without even noticing. Come, one more glass and that's enough. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I've been telling lies. Why didn't you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?"
"I knew you'd stop on your own."
"That's a lie. You did it out of spite, out of plain spite against me. You despise me. You've come here and despised me in my own house."
"Well, I'm leaving. You've had too much brandy."
"I've begged you, for Christ's sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won't go."
"I'll go tomorrow if you're so set on it."
"You won't go. You want to keep an eye on me. That's what you want, spiteful fellow. That's exactly why you won't go."
The old man kept at it. He'd reached that stage of drunkenness where a normally inoffensive drunk starts trying to pick a quarrel and assert himself.

"Why are you looking at me like that? Why do you look at me that way? Your eyes say, 'You ugly drunkard!' Your eyes are full of mistrust. They're contemptuous.... You've come here with some scheme in mind. Alyosha, here, looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn't despise me. Alexey, you mustn't love Ivan."
"Don't be so hard on my brother. Leave off attacking him," Alyosha said firmly.
"Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take the brandy away, Ivan. That's the third time I've told you."
He fell into thought, and suddenly a slow, cunning grin spread across his face.

"Don't be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don't love me, but don't be angry all the same. You've got nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I'll come and visit you myself and bring you a present. I'll show you a little wench there. I've had my eye on her a long while. She still runs around barefoot. Don't be put off by barefoot wenches -- don't despise them -- they're pearls!"
And he kissed his own hand with a smack.

"To my mind," he revived at once, seeming to grow sober the instant he touched on his favorite topic, "to my mind... Ah, you boys! You children, little sucking pigs, to my mind... I've never thought a woman ugly in my whole life -- that's been my rule! Can you understand that? How could you possibly understand it? You've got milk in your veins, not blood. You haven't even hatched yet. My rule has always been that you can find something devilishly interesting in every single woman, something you won't find in any other. Only you have to know how to find it -- that's the whole trick! That's a real talent! To my mind there's no such thing as an ugly woman. The simple fact that she's a woman is half the battle right there... but how could you understand that? Even in old maids, even in them you can discover something that makes you wonder how men could have been such fools as to let them grow old without ever noticing them. Barefoot girls, or plain ones -- you have to catch them off guard. Didn't you know that? You have to astonish them until they're dazzled, thrown off balance, ashamed that a gentleman like you could possibly fall for a little nobody like her. It's a fine thing that there always have been, and always will be, masters and servants in this world, so there'll always be some little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that's really all a man needs for happiness. Wait... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother, but in a different way. I'd pay her no attention at all, and then, all at once, when the moment came, I'd turn into pure devotion, crawl on my knees, kiss her feet, and I always, always -- I remember it like it was yesterday -- reduced her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, odd little laugh of hers. It was peculiar to her. I knew her attacks always started that way. The next day she'd start shrieking hysterically, and that little laugh wasn't a sign of pleasure at all, though it made a very convincing imitation of one. That's the great trick -- knowing how to handle every single person. Once a man named Belyavsky -- handsome fellow, and rich -- used to like coming round here and hanging about her -- suddenly gave me a slap across the face, right in front of her. And she -- meek as a lamb -- why, I thought she'd have knocked me flat for that blow. How she went at me! 'You've been struck, struck!' she said. 'You've taken a blow from him. You were trying to sell me to him,' she said.... 'And how dare he strike you in front of me! Never come near me again, never, never! Go at once, challenge him to a duel!' I took her to the monastery after that, to bring her back to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear to God, Alyosha, I never once insulted the poor crazy girl! Except once, maybe, that first year. She was very fond of praying back then. She used to observe the feasts of Our Lady especially, and would turn me out of her room on those days. I'll knock that mysticism right out of her, I thought! 'Here,' I said, 'you see this holy image of yours. Here it is. I'm taking it down. You believe it's miraculous, but here, I'll spit on it right now and nothing will happen to me for it!'... When she saw that, good Lord! I thought she'd kill me. But she just jumped up, wrung her hands, then suddenly buried her face in them, started shaking all over, and collapsed to the floor... fell in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what's the matter?"

The old man jumped up in alarm. From the moment he'd started speaking about his mother, Alyosha's face had gradually changed. He'd flushed crimson, his eyes were glowing, his lips trembling. The old sot had gone rambling on, oblivious to all of it, until the moment when something very strange happened to Alyosha. What he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly repeated in Alyosha, exactly. He jumped up from his seat exactly as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, buried his face in them, and fell back into his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, silent, violent weeping. His startling resemblance to his mother struck the old man forcefully.

"Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It's exactly like her, exactly like her, his mother. Spit some water on him, that's what I used to do for her. He's upset about his mother, his mother," he muttered to Ivan.

"But she was my mother too, I believe -- his mother. Wasn't she?" said Ivan, with unrestrained anger and contempt. The old man shrank back before his blazing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second; it seemed to have genuinely slipped the old man's mind that Alyosha's mother was Ivan's mother too.

"Your mother?" he muttered, not understanding. "What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind's never gone dark like that before. Forgive me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!" He stopped. A broad, drunken, half-senseless grin spread across his face.
At that moment a fearful noise and uproar came from the hall -- violent shouting, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man rushed to Ivan in terror.
"He'll kill me! He'll kill me! Don't let him near me!" he screamed, clutching at the skirt of Ivan's coat.
